\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec along three axes.

\paragraph{Grammar-constrained decoding.}
XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, LMQL~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql}, SynCode~\cite{ugare2024syncode}, and Grammar-Aligned Decoding~\cite{park2024grammar} guarantee format validity via CFG-based token masking; JSONSchemaBench~\cite{jsonschemabench2025} benchmarks these systems.
GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} applies grammar constraints to IE tasks.
In code generation, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} and Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022} enforce type constraints via incremental parsing, and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile full type systems into prefix automata.
These methods ensure syntactic or type-level validity but operate on static type declarations; IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, where constraint targets depend on the co-occurring relation type.
OntoCoDec's grammar layer builds on XGrammar; its semantic layer extends constrained decoding from syntax to ontology-level type enforcement.

\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} encode ontology structure as Python dataclasses and train models to generate typed code.
InstructUIE~\cite{wang2023instructuie}, DeepStruct~\cite{wang2022deepstruct}, UIE~\cite{lu2022uie}, and USM~\cite{lou2023usm} unify extraction tasks via structured output formats with task-specific training.
UniversalNER~\cite{zhou2024universalner} achieves strong zero-shot NER via targeted distillation.
\citet{wadhwa2023revisiting} benchmark LLM-based RE and find persistent schema compliance gaps.
These methods internalize constraints through training; OntoCoDec enforces them at decoding time without retraining, and the two approaches are complementary (a GoLLIE-trained model could use OntoCoDec to eliminate residual violations).

\paragraph{Constraint enforcement in IE.}
\citet{roth_yih_2004} first formulated hard type constraints for IE via integer linear programming; OntoCoDec achieves analogous enforcement within autoregressive decoding.
Post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025,slot2025} detects violations after generation and requires rejection or correction cycles.
EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} enforces structural constraints via ASP but requires hand-crafted rules; IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} supports semantic constraints via backtracking but requires manual implementation per constraint.
BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025} combines constrained and unconstrained decoding for IE.
Recent work shows constrained decoding can degrade reasoning~\cite{banerjee2025crane,schall2025hiddencost,formattax2026}; however, extraction tasks are robust to format constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak}, and OntoCoDec constrains only type tokens while leaving entity spans unconstrained.
OntoCoDec prevents violations during decoding, is training-free, and compiles constraints automatically from ontology schemas.

\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which compiles Information Extraction (IE) ontology schemas into two composable token-level decoding constraints:
(1)~a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar) that guarantees JSON structural validity and vocabulary membership; and
(2)~a \emph{semantic layer} that enforces per-triple domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations that persist after fine-tuning; violation rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} rather than ontology or model scale.
% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), \textsc{OntoCoDec} achieves near-lossless composability under fine-tuning: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp.
Under zero-shot decoding, DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models, with an accompanying cross-field consistency (CF) increase (9--21\% zero-shot, resolved to $\leq$1.2\% by fine-tuning on both RE and EE).
Beam search with LoRA eliminates all four violation types on SciERC.
The framework extends to event extraction without modification (preliminary, 20-document test set).
OntoCoDec is training-free and applies to any autoregressive LM across four models (8B--70B) and three tokenizer families.
\end{abstract}

+We present OntoCoDec, a two-layer constrained decoding framework that compiles IE schemas into token-level masks enforced during autoregressive generation.

Unlike type-constrained code generation, IE presents three distinct challenges: (1)~entity types are inferred from free text rather than declared annotations, (2)~the entity registry is built dynamically during generation, and (3)~constraint targets are context-dependent type assignments rather than fixed grammar productions.

The grammar layer (\S\ref{sec:grammar}) guarantees structural validity (well-formed JSON with ontology-vocabulary membership), while the semantic layer (\S\ref{sec:semantic}) enforces domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry.
We describe the problem formulation (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), each layer, and two decoding strategies (\S\ref{sec:strategies}).

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion (maximally compressed)
% Full discussion in Appendix; Mistral boundary condition in app:dual-factor.

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontology schemas into composable token-level decoding constraints.
The core finding is that ontology type constraints can be compiled into token-level masks that compose near-losslessly with standard fine-tuning: DR reaches $\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp on RE (R-F1 40--46), RoV$\to$0\% and AC$\leq$0.8\% on EE, and beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four RE violation types for calibrated models (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Under zero-shot decoding (R-F1 2--8\%), DR drops by 42--99\% across three models and three datasets with no significant F1 cost.

CF remains an open challenge for per-slot enforcement: the current architecture enforces type constraints independently per relation slot, so the same entity can receive different type assignments across triples.
Global entity-level type consensus during decoding, where all slots referencing the same entity must agree on its type, offers the most direct resolution path.

The framework applies to any autoregressive IE system without model modification or additional training: the constraint compiler takes an ontology schema as input and produces token-level masks compatible with any LM vocabulary.
This generality is validated across four models (8B--70B), three tokenizer families, and two IE tasks (RE, EE).
The interaction between constraint tightness and model calibration is consistent across three datasets but would benefit from validation on a broader range of ontologies and model scales.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), where extracted triples feed directly into knowledge graphs, reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs and becomes impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a framework that compiles an IE ontology into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
Our two-layer architecture reflects the observation that structural violations (malformed output, unknown types) and semantic violations (type-constraint breaches) require fundamentally different enforcement mechanisms.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.
The layers compose via bitwise AND with an \emph{enabling dependency}: the grammar layer guarantees vocabulary membership, so the semantic layer can look up domain/range rules.
Unlike type-constrained code generation where types are statically declared, IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, with constraint targets that depend on the co-occurring relation.
Composed with LoRA, OntoCoDec achieves near-lossless composability under fine-tuning: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46), our recommended deployment configuration.
Zero-shot evaluation, which stress-tests constraint robustness without task supervision (R-F1 2--8\%), confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models while remaining F1-neutral.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE: rates correlate with constraint tightness rather than ontology scale, and prompt-level intervention is per-relation unreliable.
    \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer framework compiling ontology schemas into stateful logit masks that enforce pair-based domain/range constraints during autoregressive IE, unlike code generation where types are statically declared.
    \item Near-lossless composability with LoRA on RE: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46), with CF trade-off resolved to $\leq$1.2\% by fine-tuning. Zero-shot evaluation across four models (8B--70B) confirms DR reductions of 76--99\% for calibrated models.
    \item Beam search ($k{=}4$) with LoRA eliminates all four violation types on SciERC. Preliminary extension to event extraction (WikiEvents, 20-document test set): vocabulary violations eliminated without architectural modification; fine-tuning composability analysis.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), where extracted triples feed directly into knowledge graphs, reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs and becomes impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles an IE schema into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
Our two-layer architecture reflects the observation that structural violations (malformed output, unknown types) and semantic violations (type-constraint breaches) require fundamentally different enforcement mechanisms.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.
The layers compose via bitwise AND with an \emph{enabling dependency}: the grammar layer guarantees vocabulary membership, so the semantic layer can look up domain/range rules.
Unlike type-constrained code generation where types are statically declared, IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, with constraint targets that depend on the co-occurring relation.

\label{sec:violation_landscape}

We evaluate OntoCoDec in two complementary regimes.
Fine-tuning composability (\S\ref{sec:composability}) demonstrates deployment readiness: constraints compose losslessly with standard LoRA training at R-F1 40--46, our recommended configuration.
Zero-shot evaluation stress-tests constraint robustness under adversarial conditions (no task supervision, R-F1 2--8), where CF trade-offs are expected and documented (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).

\paragraph{Setup.}
We evaluate on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) and DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 dev documents,\footnote{DocRED test annotations are not publicly available; we evaluate on the development set.} 96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$).
RE type constraints are extracted automatically from observed type pairs in training data (neither dataset provides a formal ontology); EE constraints on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}) are derived from the KAIROS ontology.
The framework handles both sources without modification.
Primary model: Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, zero-shot greedy decoding; cross-model validation in \S\ref{sec:cross-model}, composability with fine-tuning in \S\ref{sec:composability}.
We measure four violation categories: \textbf{DR} (domain/range type pair $\notin \sigma(r)$), \textbf{RV} (relation $\notin \mathcal{R}$), \textbf{ET} (entity type $\notin \mathcal{E}$), and \textbf{CF} (same entity assigned conflicting types across triples).
Baseline DR violations are 15.37\% (SciERC) and 18.46\% (DocRED), comparable rates associated with constraint tightness rather than ontology scale (\S\ref{sec:introduction}); schema-informed prompting reduces DR by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).

% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$. This reflects the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.
Among type violations, DR and CF differ in severity: a DR violation renders the triple ontologically invalid (the entity type lies outside the relation's domain or range), whereas a CF violation means each triple is individually schema-valid but the same entity receives different type assignments across triples.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
Recall the tightness of relation $r$ (\S\ref{sec:bg:ontology}):
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\sigma(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions; fallback frequency and residual DR increase accordingly.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline violation rate) is consistent with the cross-dataset results: SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction vs.\ DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) at 45--90\%; the full range across three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).
The pattern extends to WikiEvents EE ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.82$; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents-kappa}).

\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
\label{sec:rectangularity}
% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
Sequential masking is necessary because ontology type signatures are non-rectangular (0/7 SciERC, 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$); independent enforcement would admit 33--37\% spurious pairs.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Fine-tuning narrows the fallback regime: DR drops to $\leq$\,0.20\% and CF to $\leq$\,1.18\%, with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp; the grammar layer becomes a no-op and the semantic layer alone reduces residual DR by 39--72\% (\S\ref{sec:composability}).

The framework applies to any autoregressive IE system without model modification or additional training: the constraint compiler takes a schema as input and produces token-level masks compatible with any LM vocabulary.
This generality is validated across four models (8B--70B), three tokenizer families, and two IE tasks (RE, EE).
The interaction between constraint tightness and model calibration is consistent across three datasets but would benefit from validation on a broader range of ontologies and model scales.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion
% Full discussion in Appendix; Mistral boundary condition in app:dual-factor.

OntoCoDec compiles IE schemas into composable token-level decoding constraints.
The core finding is that type constraints can be compiled into token-level masks that achieve near-lossless DR composability under fine-tuning: DR reaches $\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp on RE (R-F1 40--46), CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%, RoV$\to$0\% and AC$\leq$0.8\% on EE, and beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four RE violation types for calibrated models (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Under zero-shot decoding (R-F1 2--8\%), DR drops by 42--99\% across three models and three datasets with no significant F1 cost.

The R-F1 gap between constrained fine-tuning (40--46) and supervised state-of-the-art systems (49--53~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}) traces to base model IE ability, not constraint overhead; OntoCoDec is a deployment-time constraint layer complementary to training improvements.
A GoLLIE-trained or UIE-trained model could use OntoCoDec to eliminate residual type violations that persist after training.

CF remains an open challenge for per-slot enforcement: the current architecture enforces type constraints independently per relation slot, so the same entity can receive different type assignments across triples.
Global entity-level type consensus during decoding, where all slots referencing the same entity must agree on its type, offers the most direct resolution path.
Entity type errors in the registry can also propagate to subsequent constraint decisions; grammar-first fallback partially mitigates this but does not eliminate it.

The framework applies to any autoregressive IE system without model modification or additional training: the constraint compiler takes a schema as input and produces token-level masks compatible with any LM vocabulary.
This generality is validated across four models (8B--70B), three tokenizer families, and two IE tasks (RE, EE).
Evaluating type-safety impact on downstream tasks (KG completion, QA pipelines) is future work.
The interaction between constraint tightness and model calibration is consistent across three datasets but would benefit from validation on a broader range of schemas and model scales.

## ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist: Complete Reference

### Source

Official PDF: [https://aclrollingreview.org/static/responsibleNLPresearch.pdf](https://aclrollingreview.org/static/responsibleNLPresearch.pdf)
Official guidelines page: [https://aclrollingreview.org/responsibleNLPresearch/](https://aclrollingreview.org/responsibleNLPresearch/)
LaTeX template repo: [https://github.com/acl-org/responsibleNLPresearch](https://github.com/acl-org/responsibleNLPresearch) (file: `templates/responsibleNLPresearch.tex`)
Published example: [https://aclanthology.org/attachments/2025.emnlp-main.1549.checklist.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/attachments/2025.emnlp-main.1549.checklist.pdf)

### Desk Rejection Policy

Starting December 2024 ARR cycle, **submissions that systematically fail to provide either specific relevant sections or justification to the questions relevant for their research will be desk-rejected**. The checklist is published as an appendix to accepted papers (EMNLP 2025 onward and all future *ACL conferences). Checklists do **not** count against page limits.

### Response Format

For each question:
- **Yes** -> provide the section number(s) where the information appears (main paper or supplemental)
- **No** -> provide a justification explaining why
- **N/A** -> indicate the question does not apply

Multiple questions may point to the same section. Answering "No" with proper justification is **not** grounds for rejection. The checklist must **not** be modified, reordered, or have questions deleted/added.

---

### Complete Checklist Items (22 questions total)

#### Section A: For Every Submission (mandatory, 3 questions)

**A1. Did you discuss the *limitations* of your work?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Discuss strong assumptions and robustness to violations; reflect on scope of claims (number of datasets, languages, runs); if analyzing biases, state definition explicitly; acknowledge limitations honestly rather than letting reviewers discover them.

**A2. Did you discuss any potential *risks* of your work?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Consider malicious/harmful effects (disinformation, fake profiles, surveillance); environmental impact; fairness considerations; privacy/security; overgeneralization across languages/topics; impact on vulnerable communities; dual-use scenarios; mitigation strategies.

**A3. Do the abstract and introduction summarize the paper's main claims?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Ensure claims are clearly stated and scoped appropriately.

#### Section B: Scientific Artifacts (gating question + 6 sub-questions)

**B. Did you use or create *scientific artifacts*?**
- Options: Yes / No (gating; if No, skip B1-B6)

**B1. Did you cite the creators of artifacts you used?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: For composite artifacts (e.g., GLUE), cite all creators; cite original papers for code/datasets; state version numbers; include URLs when possible.

**B2. Did you discuss the *license or terms* for use and/or distribution of any artifacts?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Name specific licenses (e.g., CC-BY 4.0); for scraped data state copyright and ToS; include license info for released assets; state original and derived licenses for repackaged data.

**B3. Did you discuss if your use of existing artifact(s) was consistent with their *intended use*, provided that it was specified? For the artifacts you create, do you specify intended use and whether that is compatible with the original access conditions (in particular, derivatives of data accessed for research purposes should not be used outside of research contexts)?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Verify license compatibility; specify intended use for created artifacts; address anonymization sufficiency; discuss harms from data collection limitations.

**B4. Did you discuss the steps taken to check whether the data that was collected/used contains any *information that names or uniquely identifies individual people* or *offensive content*, and the steps taken to protect / anonymize it?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Explain checking methods (script, manual sample, etc.); describe anonymization (hashing, replacement, removal); list privacy protection measures; address identifiability risks.

**B5. Did you provide documentation of the artifacts, e.g., coverage of domains, languages, and linguistic phenomena, demographic groups represented, etc.?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Report language info even for common benchmarks; describe domain, author demographics; use data statements, model cards, or datasheets.

**B6. Did you report relevant statistics like the number of examples, details of train/test/dev splits, etc. for the data that you used/created?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Report even for commonly-used benchmarks; include train/test/dev split details.

#### Section C: Computational Experiments (gating question + 4 sub-questions)

**C. Did you run *computational experiments*?**
- Options: Yes / No (gating; if No, skip C1-C4)

**C1. Did you report the *number of parameters* in the models used, the *total computational budget* (e.g., GPU hours), and *computing infrastructure* used?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Include GPU hours, parallelism details, GPU sizes; cover all experiments not just final runs; estimates acceptable.

**C2. Did you discuss the experimental setup, including *hyperparameter search* and *best-found hyperparameter* values?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Model selection procedures; data preprocessing details; hyperparameter search methods; best-found values (learning rate, regularization, etc.); specify which dataset determined hyperparameters.

**C3. Did you report *descriptive statistics* about your results (e.g., error bars around results, summary statistics from sets of experiments), and is it transparent whether you are reporting the max, mean, etc. or just a single run?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Error bars or confidence intervals; clarify max/mean/single run; include validation with test set results; use multiple random seeds.

**C4. If you used existing packages (e.g., for preprocessing, for normalization, or for evaluation), did you report the implementation, model, and parameter settings used (e.g., NLTK, Spacy, ROUGE, etc.)?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Version numbers; cite original works or provide repo URLs; explain modifications; note that different implementations yield different results.

#### Section D: Human Annotators (gating question + 5 sub-questions)

**D. Did you use *human annotators* (e.g., crowdworkers) or *research with human subjects*?**
- Options: Yes / No (gating; if No, skip D1-D5)

**D1. Did you report the full text of instructions given to participants, including e.g., screenshots, disclaimers of any risks to participants or annotators, etc.?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Full instructions including screenshots; disclaimers of risks (offensive content, PII collection).

**D2. Did you report information about how you recruited (e.g., crowdsourcing platform, students) and paid participants, and discuss if such *payment is adequate* given the participants' demographic (e.g., country of residence)?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Specific platform or recruitment method; payment amounts including bonuses; time estimates; wage fairness discussion by demographic.

**D3. Did you discuss whether and how *consent* was obtained from people whose data you're using/curating (e.g., did your instructions explain how the data would be used)?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Explain consent process; clarify if workers understood data usage.

**D4. Was the data collection protocol *approved (or determined exempt)* by an ethics review board?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Secure IRB or equivalent approval; clearly state in paper; note approval doesn't eliminate societal impact discussion requirement.

**D5. Did you report the basic demographic and geographic characteristics of the *annotator* population that is the source of the data?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Basic demographic and geographic characteristics; identify protected information; use data statements; distinguish self-reported vs. inferred.

#### Section E: AI Assistants (gating question + 1 sub-question)

**E. Did you use *AI assistants* (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot) in your research, coding, or writing?**
- Options: Yes / No (gating; if No, skip E1)

**E1. Did you include information about your use of AI assistants?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Disclose usage scope (writing, coding, research); conform with ACL authorship criteria and publications ethics policy.

---

### LaTeX Template

The official fillable LaTeX template is at `https://github.com/acl-org/responsibleNLPresearch/blob/main/templates/responsibleNLPresearch.tex`. It uses PDF form fields (`\ChoiceMenu`, `\TextField`, `\CheckBox` from the `hyperref` package). Key custom commands:

- `\cm{name}{Yes,No,N/A}{}` for radio button choice menus
- `\tf[0.85]{name}{}` for text field justifications
- `\cb{name}` for checkboxes

**Important note**: The GitHub template file may be slightly behind the official PDF (the GitHub version I retrieved does not include Section E on AI assistants). The official PDF from `aclrollingreview.org/static/responsibleNLPresearch.pdf` is the authoritative version with all 5 sections (A-E). For EMNLP 2026 submission, Section E must be included.

For embedding in the paper as an appendix (the current requirement for accepted papers), the checklist is typically filled via the OpenReview submission form and auto-generated as an appendix. Authors should fill it during submission, not manually append LaTeX.</result>

## ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist: Complete Reference

### Source

Official PDF: [https://aclrollingreview.org/static/responsibleNLPresearch.pdf](https://aclrollingreview.org/static/responsibleNLPresearch.pdf)
Official guidelines page: [https://aclrollingreview.org/responsibleNLPresearch/](https://aclrollingreview.org/responsibleNLPresearch/)
LaTeX template repo: [https://github.com/acl-org/responsibleNLPresearch](https://github.com/acl-org/responsibleNLPresearch) (file: `templates/responsibleNLPresearch.tex`)
Published example: [https://aclanthology.org/attachments/2025.emnlp-main.1549.checklist.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/attachments/2025.emnlp-main.1549.checklist.pdf)

### Desk Rejection Policy

Starting December 2024 ARR cycle, **submissions that systematically fail to provide either specific relevant sections or justification to the questions relevant for their research will be desk-rejected**. The checklist is published as an appendix to accepted papers (EMNLP 2025 onward and all future *ACL conferences). Checklists do **not** count against page limits.

### Response Format

For each question:
- **Yes** -> provide the section number(s) where the information appears (main paper or supplemental)
- **No** -> provide a justification explaining why
- **N/A** -> indicate the question does not apply

Multiple questions may point to the same section. Answering "No" with proper justification is **not** grounds for rejection. The checklist must **not** be modified, reordered, or have questions deleted/added.

---

### Complete Checklist Items (22 questions total)

#### Section A: For Every Submission (mandatory, 3 questions)

**A1. Did you discuss the *limitations* of your work?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Discuss strong assumptions and robustness to violations; reflect on scope of claims (number of datasets, languages, runs); if analyzing biases, state definition explicitly; acknowledge limitations honestly rather than letting reviewers discover them.

**A2. Did you discuss any potential *risks* of your work?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Consider malicious/harmful effects (disinformation, fake profiles, surveillance); environmental impact; fairness considerations; privacy/security; overgeneralization across languages/topics; impact on vulnerable communities; dual-use scenarios; mitigation strategies.

**A3. Do the abstract and introduction summarize the paper's main claims?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Ensure claims are clearly stated and scoped appropriately.

#### Section B: Scientific Artifacts (gating question + 6 sub-questions)

**B. Did you use or create *scientific artifacts*?**
- Options: Yes / No (gating; if No, skip B1-B6)

**B1. Did you cite the creators of artifacts you used?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: For composite artifacts (e.g., GLUE), cite all creators; cite original papers for code/datasets; state version numbers; include URLs when possible.

**B2. Did you discuss the *license or terms* for use and/or distribution of any artifacts?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Name specific licenses (e.g., CC-BY 4.0); for scraped data state copyright and ToS; include license info for released assets; state original and derived licenses for repackaged data.

**B3. Did you discuss if your use of existing artifact(s) was consistent with their *intended use*, provided that it was specified? For the artifacts you create, do you specify intended use and whether that is compatible with the original access conditions (in particular, derivatives of data accessed for research purposes should not be used outside of research contexts)?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Verify license compatibility; specify intended use for created artifacts; address anonymization sufficiency; discuss harms from data collection limitations.

**B4. Did you discuss the steps taken to check whether the data that was collected/used contains any *information that names or uniquely identifies individual people* or *offensive content*, and the steps taken to protect / anonymize it?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Explain checking methods (script, manual sample, etc.); describe anonymization (hashing, replacement, removal); list privacy protection measures; address identifiability risks.

**B5. Did you provide documentation of the artifacts, e.g., coverage of domains, languages, and linguistic phenomena, demographic groups represented, etc.?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Report language info even for common benchmarks; describe domain, author demographics; use data statements, model cards, or datasheets.

**B6. Did you report relevant statistics like the number of examples, details of train/test/dev splits, etc. for the data that you used/created?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Report even for commonly-used benchmarks; include train/test/dev split details.

#### Section C: Computational Experiments (gating question + 4 sub-questions)

**C. Did you run *computational experiments*?**
- Options: Yes / No (gating; if No, skip C1-C4)

**C1. Did you report the *number of parameters* in the models used, the *total computational budget* (e.g., GPU hours), and *computing infrastructure* used?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Include GPU hours, parallelism details, GPU sizes; cover all experiments not just final runs; estimates acceptable.

**C2. Did you discuss the experimental setup, including *hyperparameter search* and *best-found hyperparameter* values?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Model selection procedures; data preprocessing details; hyperparameter search methods; best-found values (learning rate, regularization, etc.); specify which dataset determined hyperparameters.

**C3. Did you report *descriptive statistics* about your results (e.g., error bars around results, summary statistics from sets of experiments), and is it transparent whether you are reporting the max, mean, etc. or just a single run?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Error bars or confidence intervals; clarify max/mean/single run; include validation with test set results; use multiple random seeds.

**C4. If you used existing packages (e.g., for preprocessing, for normalization, or for evaluation), did you report the implementation, model, and parameter settings used (e.g., NLTK, Spacy, ROUGE, etc.)?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Version numbers; cite original works or provide repo URLs; explain modifications; note that different implementations yield different results.

#### Section D: Human Annotators (gating question + 5 sub-questions)

**D. Did you use *human annotators* (e.g., crowdworkers) or *research with human subjects*?**
- Options: Yes / No (gating; if No, skip D1-D5)

**D1. Did you report the full text of instructions given to participants, including e.g., screenshots, disclaimers of any risks to participants or annotators, etc.?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Full instructions including screenshots; disclaimers of risks (offensive content, PII collection).

**D2. Did you report information about how you recruited (e.g., crowdsourcing platform, students) and paid participants, and discuss if such *payment is adequate* given the participants' demographic (e.g., country of residence)?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Specific platform or recruitment method; payment amounts including bonuses; time estimates; wage fairness discussion by demographic.

**D3. Did you discuss whether and how *consent* was obtained from people whose data you're using/curating (e.g., did your instructions explain how the data would be used)?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Explain consent process; clarify if workers understood data usage.

**D4. Was the data collection protocol *approved (or determined exempt)* by an ethics review board?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Secure IRB or equivalent approval; clearly state in paper; note approval doesn't eliminate societal impact discussion requirement.

**D5. Did you report the basic demographic and geographic characteristics of the *annotator* population that is the source of the data?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Basic demographic and geographic characteristics; identify protected information; use data statements; distinguish self-reported vs. inferred.

#### Section E: AI Assistants (gating question + 1 sub-question)

**E. Did you use *AI assistants* (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot) in your research, coding, or writing?**
- Options: Yes / No (gating; if No, skip E1)

**E1. Did you include information about your use of AI assistants?**
- Options: Yes / No / N/A
- Guidelines: Disclose usage scope (writing, coding, research); conform with ACL authorship criteria and publications ethics policy.

---

### LaTeX Template

The official fillable LaTeX template is at `https://github.com/acl-org/responsibleNLPresearch/blob/main/templates/responsibleNLPresearch.tex`. It uses PDF form fields (`\ChoiceMenu`, `\TextField`, `\CheckBox` from the `hyperref` package). Key custom commands:

- `\cm{name}{Yes,No,N/A}{}` for radio button choice menus
- `\tf[0.85]{name}{}` for text field justifications
- `\cb{name}` for checkboxes

**Important note**: The GitHub template file may be slightly behind the official PDF (the GitHub version I retrieved does not include Section E on AI assistants). The official PDF from `aclrollingreview.org/static/responsibleNLPresearch.pdf` is the authoritative version with all 5 sections (A-E). For EMNLP 2026 submission, Section E must be included.

For embedding in the paper as an appendix (the current requirement for accepted papers), the checklist is typically filled via the OpenReview submission form and auto-generated as an appendix. Authors should fill it during submission, not manually append LaTeX.</result>

1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user is the Director of an ML research project (`schema_semantic_constrained_ie`), directing a Paper Agent to prepare the EMNLP 2026 paper "OntoCoDec" for submission via ARR. This session covers:
   - **Completing Round 8 数据集成 reporting** (verifying pages ≤ 8, reporting to Director)

   - **Round 9 审稿修复 — 12 tasks** across P0/P1/P2 priorities (all completed)

   - **Round 10 审稿修复 — 16 tasks** (currently in progress, ~10/16 done)

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - OntoCoDec: Two-layer constrained decoding (grammar + semantic) for IE
   - "near-lossless DR composability" (previously "near-lossless composability") — the key framing change
   - FT = deployment recommendation, ZS = stress-test for constraint robustness
   - CF (Cross-Field consistency) trade-off: 9-21% zero-shot, resolved to ≤1.2% by fine-tuning
   - Constraint tightness κ: SciERC κ̄=0.333, DocRED κ̄=0.842, WikiEvents κ̄=0.82
   - Title changed from "Compiled Ontology Constraints" → "Compiled Schema Constraints"
   - "Ontology schemas" → "schemas" throughout (broad definition kept in §2 only)
   - OntoCoDec expansion removed (no longer "Ontology-Compiled Decoding")
   - Contributions reduced from 4 to 3; EE demoted to preliminary mention within C3
   - ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist: 22 questions in sections A-E, required for desk reject prevention
   - EMNLP 2026 via ARR: 8-page main body limit

3. Files and Code Sections:

   - **`artifacts/_project/paper/main.tex`**
     - Title change (Task 1), needs \input{checklist} added (Task 4 pending)
     ```latex
     \title{OntoCoDec: Type-Constrained Information Extraction\\via Compiled Schema Constraints}
     ```

   - **`artifacts/_project/paper/abstract.tex`** (Final state after Round 10)
     - Multiple rewrites: CF scope expansion, Round 9 full rewrite (~175 words, ≤5 numbers), Round 10 "schemas" + "DR composability"
     ```latex
     \begin{abstract}
     We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which compiles Information Extraction (IE) schemas into two composable token-level decoding constraints:
     (1)~a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar) that guarantees JSON structural validity and vocabulary membership; and
     (2)~a \emph{semantic layer} that enforces per-triple domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
     Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations that persist after fine-tuning; violation rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} rather than ontology or model scale.
     % exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
     Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), \textsc{OntoCoDec} achieves near-lossless DR composability under fine-tuning: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%.
     Under zero-shot decoding, DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models, with an accompanying cross-field consistency (CF) increase (9--21\% zero-shot, resolved to $\leq$1.2\% by fine-tuning on both RE and EE).
     Beam search with LoRA eliminates all four violation types on SciERC.
     The framework extends to event extraction without modification (preliminary, 20-document test set).
     OntoCoDec is training-free and applies to any autoregressive LM across four models (8B--70B) and three tokenizer families.
     \end{abstract}
     ```

   - **`artifacts/_project/paper/section1_introduction_draft.tex`** (Final state after Round 10)
     - Task 2: Removed OntoCoDec expansion `(\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding)`
     - Task 3: "ontology schemas" → "schemas", "IE ontology" → "IE schema"
     - Task 5: "near-lossless composability" → "near-lossless DR composability", added CF ≤1.2%
     - Task 6: Contributions 4→3
     ```latex
     We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles an IE schema into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
     ```
     ```latex
     Composed with LoRA, OntoCoDec achieves near-lossless DR composability under fine-tuning: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46), CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%, our recommended deployment configuration.
     ```
     Contributions now:
     ```latex
     \item An empirical characterization of type violations in LLM-based IE across 103 relations: violation rates correlate with constraint tightness rather than schema scale, and prompt-level intervention is per-relation unreliable.
     \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer framework compiling IE schemas into stateful logit masks that enforce pair-based domain/range constraints during autoregressive IE, unlike code generation where types are statically declared.
     \item Near-lossless DR composability with LoRA on RE: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost (R-F1 40--46), with CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%. Zero-shot evaluation across four models (8B--70B) confirms DR reductions of 76--99\% for calibrated models. Beam search ($k{=}4$) with LoRA eliminates all four violation types on SciERC. The framework extends to event extraction without modification (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}, preliminary).
     ```

   - **`artifacts/_project/paper/section2_background.tex`**
     - MF2 ontology definition expansion + constraint coverage data
     ```latex
     We quantify constraint restrictiveness via \emph{constraint tightness} $\kappa(r)$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:tightness}, \S\ref{sec:composition}): tighter constraints leave fewer valid type pairs per relation.
     We define ontology constraints broadly to encompass both formal ontology specifications (e.g., the KAIROS event ontology with explicit role-entity type mappings) and empirically derived type-pair constraints extracted from annotated training data.
     The latter applies when datasets lack a formal ontology but provide typed annotations (SciERC, DocRED); OntoCoDec compiles both sources into the same constraint representation without modification.
     Empirical constraints achieve 99\%+ instance-level coverage on held-out data (SciERC 99.0\%, DocRED 99.4\%); uncovered type pairs trigger grammar-first fallback (\S\ref{sec:composition}), ensuring no valid triples are blocked.
     ```

   - **`artifacts/_project/paper/section3_violation_landscape.tex`** (§5 framing)
     - Task 8: Rewritten framing paragraph
     ```latex
     We evaluate OntoCoDec in two regimes.
     Fine-tuning composability (\S\ref{sec:composability}) tests the recommended deployment configuration: LoRA + S1 constraints at R-F1 40--46.
     Zero-shot evaluation (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}--\S\ref{sec:cross-model}) isolates layer contributions and stress-tests constraint robustness without task supervision; R-F1 2--8 reflects the absence of task-specific training, not method failure.
     ```

     - Task 3: "ontology schemas" → "IE schemas"

     - Task 12 (Round 9): Dedup with §2, changed to "Recall the tightness" + unified $\sigma(r)$ notation

     ```latex
     \paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
     Recall the tightness of relation $r$ (\S\ref{sec:bg:ontology}):\footnote{For symmetric relations, $|\sigma(r)|$ counts ordered pairs; the normalization $|\mathcal{E}|^2$ remains appropriate since we evaluate on directed triples.}
     ```

   - **`artifacts/_project/paper/section5_scierc_draft.tex`** — NOT YET MODIFIED in Round 10. Tasks 9, 10, 11 pending (FT paragraph expansion, DocRED rows in Table 2, Bootstrap CI).

   - **`artifacts/_project/paper/section5_crossmodel_draft.tex`**
     - Round 9 SF1: Post-hoc filtering comparison paragraph
     - Round 9 SF4: Mistral boundary condition paragraph
     ```latex
     \paragraph{Mistral as boundary condition.}
     Effective semantic constraint enforcement presupposes that the base model assigns entity types within the ontology vocabulary.
     When entity typing quality degrades substantially (Mistral: ET 1.5--7.6\% unconstrained, DR 56.9--57.4\%), the semantic layer cannot correct entity misclassification errors that precede constraint application; DR reduction is limited to 42\% vs.\ 76--99\% for calibrated models.

     \paragraph{Post-hoc filtering comparison.}
     Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in 5/6 zero-shot settings through precision gains (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}), but at rejection rates of 15--74\%, discarding substantial correct predictions.
     Under fine-tuning, both methods achieve comparable F1.
     OntoCoDec and post-hoc filtering target different operating points: post-hoc suits precision-critical applications willing to sacrifice recall; OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation.
     ```

     The increase in Llama parse failures under constraints (6.8\%\,$\to$\,9.1\%) reflects an inherent trade-off: constraint masking alters token probability distributions, which can push generation toward suboptimal paths in long documents.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion
% Full discussion in Appendix; Mistral boundary condition in app:dual-factor.

OntoCoDec compiles IE schemas into composable token-level decoding constraints.
The core finding is that type constraints can be compiled into token-level masks that achieve near-lossless DR composability under fine-tuning: DR reaches $\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp on RE (R-F1 40--46), CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%, RoV$\to$0\% and AC$\leq$0.8\% on EE, and beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four RE violation types for calibrated models (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Under zero-shot decoding (R-F1 2--8\%), DR drops by 42--99\% across three models and three datasets with no significant F1 cost.

The R-F1 gap between constrained fine-tuning (40--46) and supervised state-of-the-art systems (49--53~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}) traces to base model IE ability, not constraint overhead; OntoCoDec is a deployment-time constraint layer complementary to training improvements.
A GoLLIE-trained or UIE-trained model could use OntoCoDec to eliminate residual type violations that persist after training.

CF remains an open challenge for per-slot enforcement: the current architecture enforces type constraints independently per relation slot, so the same entity can receive different type assignments across triples.
Global entity-level type consensus during decoding, where all slots referencing the same entity must agree on its type, offers the most direct resolution path.
Entity type errors in the registry can also propagate to subsequent constraint decisions; grammar-first fallback partially mitigates this but does not eliminate it.

The framework applies to any autoregressive IE system without model modification or additional training: the constraint compiler takes a schema as input and produces token-level masks compatible with any LM vocabulary.
This generality is validated across four models (8B--70B), three tokenizer families, and two IE tasks (RE, EE).
Evaluating type-safety impact on downstream tasks (KG completion, QA pipelines) is future work.
The interaction between constraint tightness and model calibration is consistent across three datasets but would benefit from validation on a broader range of schemas and model scales.

% Section 5 — DocRED Results (compressed, 1450→~600 words)
% exp_ids: phase2_docred_unconstrained, phase2_docred_grammar_only,
%          phase2_docred_semantic_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Validation on DocRED}
\label{sec:docred-results}

Table~\ref{tab:docred-ablation} presents the four-way ablation on DocRED (96 Wikidata relation types, 14$\times$ SciERC; Qwen3-8B, zero-shot, 998 documents).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: DocRED four-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{6}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-7} \cmidrule(l){8-9}
\textbf{Mode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$DR
  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF & Tot.\,$\downarrow$
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
Unconstrained
  & 18.46 & ---
  & 29.66 & 2.48
  & 0.10  & 18.56
  & 7.74  & 58.15 \\
Grammar
  & 26.17 & $\uparrow$42\%
  & \textbf{0.03} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.07  & 26.24
  & \textbf{8.31}  & \textbf{59.38} \\
Semantic
  & 13.84 & $\downarrow$25\%
  & 29.87 & 4.22
  & 1.05  & 14.89
  & 7.70  & 57.81 \\
Full (S1)
  & \textbf{10.21} & $\downarrow$\textbf{45\%}
  & \textbf{0.03} & \textbf{0}
  & 2.57  & \textbf{12.78}
  & 8.23  & 59.37 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Four-way ablation on DocRED (998 documents, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
$\Delta$DR: relative change vs.\ unconstrained.
Tot.\ = DR + CF (total type-violation burden).
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded; Tot.\ included).
F1 $\times$100. Bootstrap significance: R-F1 $+$0.50\,pp ($p < 0.001$).}
\label{tab:docred-ablation}
\end{table}

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_unconstrained, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}
Full S1 reduces DR from 18.46\% to 10.21\% ($\downarrow$45\%), eliminates ET ($\to$\,0\%), and near-eliminates RV (29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%).\footnote{The residual 0.03\% RV traces to a rare XGrammar automaton edge case where subword tokens from different enum entries combine into chimeric values (e.g., \texttt{member} + \texttt{icipant\_of} from \texttt{member\_of} and \texttt{participant\_of}). This is not a fundamental limitation of the approach.}
R-F1 improves from 7.74 to 8.23 ($+$0.50\,pp; $p < 0.001$), attributable to elimination of 5{,}189 OOV relation predictions.
CF increases modestly (0.10\%\,$\to$\,2.57\%), consistent with the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_grammar_only, phase2_docred_semantic_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Layer contributions.}
Grammar-only eliminates RV and ET but \emph{increases} DR to 26.17\%: OOV triples (29.66\% baseline) become evaluable and expose latent type incompatibilities.
Semantic-only reduces DR by 25\% but cannot eliminate RV or ET, the same enabling dependency observed on SciERC.
Residual DR (10.21\% vs.\ SciERC's 0.93\%) reflects higher tightness ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$ vs.\ 0.333), which forces frequent fallback; effective semantic coverage is $\sim$90\% (Appendix~\ref{app:fallback-coverage}).
Under fine-tuning, residual narrows to 0.01--0.20\% (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
The increase in Llama parse failures under constraints (6.8\%\,$\to$\,9.1\%) reflects an inherent trade-off: constraint masking alters token probability distributions, which can push generation toward suboptimal paths in long documents.

% Section 5 — Event Extraction on WikiEvents (compact, inline)
% exp_ids: ee_qwen_wikievents_unconstrained, ee_llama_wikievents_unconstrained,
%          ee_mistral_wikievents_unconstrained, ee_qwen_wikievents_constrained,
%          ee_llama_wikievents_constrained, ee_mistral_wikievents_constrained_v2
% v3 final data confirmed by Director 2026-05-18.

\subsection{Preliminary Extension: Event Extraction}
\label{sec:wikievents}

We apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} (56 event types, 80 roles, 27 entity types, 245 constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}) without modification.
Violations extend to EV (event vocabulary), RoV (role vocabulary), and AC (argument constraint, analogous to DR).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: WikiEvents three-model comparison (v3 final)
%  exp_ids: ee_{qwen,llama,mistral}_wikievents_{unconstrained,grammar_only,constrained_v3}
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.8pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll rrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{4}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Mode}
  & EV\,$\downarrow$ & RoV\,$\downarrow$ & AC & CF
  & Trig.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Qwen3-8B}
  & Unconstr.\ & 24.0 & 74.9 & 0.3 & 0 & 11.8 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 76.1 & 8.2 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 2.1 & 21.1 & 13.4 & 14.1 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{Llama\\3.1-8B}}
  & Unconstr.\ & 10.5 & 88.8 & 0.1 & 0 & 5.7 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 77.0 & 8.8 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 3.8 & 17.2 & 7.5 & 17.6 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{Mistral\\7B}}
  & Unconstr.\ & 37.3 & 63.9 & 0 & 0 & 2.4 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 64.0 & 13.8 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & Full S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 1.3 & 14.9 & 3.9 & 11.7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{WikiEvents EE results (246 documents, zero-shot).
Violation rates over parsed documents.
---: not applicable (grammar-only has no semantic-layer metrics).
F1 $\times$ 100.}
\label{tab:wikievents}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Results.}
Unconstrained EE produces extreme vocabulary violations (EV+RoV $>$85\%; Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}), with entity F1\,=\,0 because the parser cannot process off-schema output.
Full S1 eliminates EV and RoV across all models, which validates the tokenizer-agnostic design across byte-level BPE and SentencePiece.
Grammar-only eliminates EV but leaves RoV at 64--77\% and surfaces latent AC (8--14\%), consistent with DocRED's pattern (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}); full S1 drives RoV to 0\%.
Residual AC (1.3--3.8\%) traces to semantically similar types (e.g., SID vs.\ SEN).
CF rises to 15--21\%, exceeding RE levels (10--12\%) because EE's multi-argument structures increase entity reuse across slots.
Post-hoc filtering is impractical ($<$0.5\% arguments retained).
Unlike RE, EE shows measurable F1 gains: entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%, trigger F1 $+$1.5--1.8\,pp.

% exp_ids: p1_ee_ft_qwen_wikievents_r5, p1_ee_ft_llama_wikievents_r5
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning (preliminary).}
WikiEvents uses a 194/20/20 train/dev/test split~\cite{li2021document}; the 20-document test set is a dataset constraint, not a design choice.
LoRA + S1 eliminates RoV (Qwen 38.31\%\,$\to$\,0\%, Llama 8.8\%\,$\to$\,0\%; bootstrap 95\% CI [0\%,\,0\%] and [0\%,\,1.73\%]) and reduces AC to $\leq$0.8\%, with argument F1 within $\pm$1.1\,pp; trigger F1 shows larger shifts ($-$5.4/$-$0.6\,pp) with wide confidence intervals at this sample size.
CF remains low under fine-tuning (0.77--1.18\%), consistent with RE composability results (\S\ref{sec:composition}, Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Constrained decoding does not further reduce EE CF because the semantic layer enforces per-event role-type compatibility but not cross-event entity type consensus, the same architectural limitation identified in RE (\S\ref{sec:composition}).

% Data source: Phase 2 SciERC registry experiments
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_grammar_only,
%          phase2_scierc_semantic_only, phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_scierc_full_s2
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Ablation and Composability with Fine-Tuning}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot, 551 documents); only the active constraint layers differ across rows.

Grammar-only represents the ceiling of grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}: vocabulary membership is enforced but cross-field semantic constraints are not.}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
Full S1 reduces DR from 15.37\% to 0.93\% ($\downarrow$94\%) while R-F1 is unchanged (8.23\,$\to$\,8.36, $p{=}0.58$).
Per-relation DR drops to $\leq$2.82\%, reaching 0\% on 4/7 relations (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).
Post-hoc filtering achieves slightly higher F1 via precision gains but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}).
CF rises from 0.08\% to 9.90\% (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Layer contributions.}
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823
Grammar-only eliminates RV and ET with no F1 impact while DR remains at 14.84\%, the ceiling of grammar-based decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}; grammar-only CF is near-zero (0.08\%), so CF originates from the semantic layer.
Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% and cannot eliminate RV or ET; this is the \emph{enabling dependency}: adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval
Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Adding S1: Qwen DR 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\%, Llama 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\% on SciERC; Qwen 0.76\%\,$\to$\,0.01\%, Llama 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0.20\% on DocRED.
% w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.01%, R-F1=40.56; w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.20%, R-F1=44.23
Across all settings, DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp.
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X ambiguity (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates residual DR and CF to $<$1\% (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).
